results.title: GPU Cloud Rental Prices 2026: H100 vs H200 Cost Comparison | GPUSmith
highlights:
As of July 2026, renting an NVIDIA H100 GPU in the cloud costs between roughly $1.38 and $6.98 per GPU-hour depending on provider, with a cross-provider median near $2.99/hr, while the newer H200 (141GB HBM3e memory) runs from about $2.30 to $13.78/hr with a median around $4.00 [1]. The single biggest driver of price is provider category, not the chip itself: specialized "neocloud" providers such as Runpod ($1.99 to $2.39/hr for H100 PCIe) [2], Lambda ($3.99/hr on-demand H100 SXM) [3], Vast.ai (from $1.38/hr on a peer-to-peer marketplace), and Nebius ($3.85/hr H100, $4.50/hr H200 as of June 2026) [4] undercut the three major hyperscalers by roughly 40% to 400%. Microsoft Azure lists its NC40ads H100 v5 instance at $6.98/hr on-demand (Source: instances.vantage.sh), AWS prices its p5.4xlarge (1x H100) at $6.88/hr [5], and Google Cloud's A3 Mega H100 instance runs $93.40/hr for 8 GPUs, or roughly $11.68/GPU-hour [6].

The pricing gap between "neocloud" specialists and hyperscalers reflects fundamentally different business models rather than different hardware: the underlying silicon is identical NVIDIA Hopper-generation compute in both cases. Analysis from Spheron found that "an H100 on Spheron starts at $1.33/hr compared to $6.98/hr on Azure and $7.00/hr on AWS (as of Q1 2026), that's 40 to 60% less than hyperscalers" (Source: spheron.network). The independent research firm SemiAnalysis documents a separate and more volatile trend in the committed-capacity market: 1-year H100 rental contract pricing "shot up almost 40% from a low of $1.70/hr/GPU in October 2025 to $2.35/hr/GPU by March 2026" [7], driven by surging inference demand from multi-agent AI workloads even as on-demand spot pricing has continued to soften.

...

Buyers evaluating GPU cloud rental prices should treat "H100 pricing" and "H200 pricing" as ranges bounded by provider category rather than single numbers: marketplace and neocloud on-demand rates cluster in the $1.38 to $4.50 range for both chips, while hyperscaler on-demand list prices run $6.88 to over $13 per GPU-hour [10]. Reserved and multi-year contracts, spot/preemptible instances, and per-second versus per-hour billing further widen the effective spread, and this report walks through each of these levers in detail, alongside named deployments from CoreWeave, Corvex, and Mistral AI that illustrate how enterprises are actually buying this capacity in mid-2026.

...

Pricing volatility has been the defining story of this market since late 2025. SemiAnalysis, an independent semiconductor and AI infrastructure research firm, reports that "on-demand GPU rental capacity is sold out across all GPU types" as of early 2026, with providers unwilling to relinquish locked-up on-demand instances even as list prices rise [7]. At the same time, the AIMultiple Cloud GPU Rental Price Index, which tracks 63 providers and 17 GPU models monthly, finds that posted on-demand median pricing for mainstream Hopper-generation cards has held in a relatively tight band even as newer Blackwell cards saw sharper increases [1]. These two data sources are not contradictory: they measure different segments of the same market, on-demand posted list pricing versus negotiated committed-capacity contracts, and the divergence between them is itself one of the most important facts a buyer needs to understand before committing budget.

...

AWS cut P5 on-demand pricing by 44% in June 2025, a move widely covered in trade press as a response to intensifying competition from neocloud providers (Source: www.spheron.network). Despite the cut, AWS remains the default choice for organizations already standardized on AWS services such as SageMaker, Bedrock, or EFA-optimized EKS clusters, where migrating workloads to a neocloud carries real integration costs.

...

GCP also lists

...

The "neocloud" category, providers built specifically around GPU rental rather than general-purpose cloud services, spans a wide range of pricing models. Runpod offers H100 PCIe "from $1.99/hr on Community Cloud and $2.39/hr on Secure Cloud" [2], with H200 SXM starting at $3.59/hr on Community Cloud [10]. Lambda prices on-demand H100 SXM at $3.99 to $4.29/hr depending on cluster size and region, with its 1-Click Cluster product offering $6.16/hr per GPU for a 16-GPU reserved H100 cluster on a 2-week to 1-year term, dropping to $5.54/hr at 256-GPU scale [3]. Vast.ai, a peer-to-peer GPU marketplace, rents H200 GPUs "for $3.75/hr" [18] and lists H100 on-demand pricing in the $1.38 to $1.87/hr range according to independent tracking [13]. CoreWeave lists an 8-GPU HGX H100 node at $49.24/hr on-demand ($6.16/GPU-hour) with spot pricing at $19.71/hr ($2.46/GPU-hour), and an 8-GPU HGX H200 node at $50.44/hr on-demand ($6.31/GPU-hour) [19]. Nebius raised prices effective June 1, 2026, moving on-demand H100 NVLink from $2.95/hr to $3.85/hr and H200 NVLink from $3.50/hr to $4.50/hr, while preemptible H100 rose from $1.25/hr to $2.15/hr [4]. Jarvislabs advertises H100 at $2.69/hr and H200 at $3.80/hr, described independently as an "under-the-radar provider with competitive pricing" offering "under-90-second instance spin-up" and per-minute billing [13].

...

How a provider bills for GPU time changes the effective price as much as the headline rate does. Three billing models dominate the market. On-demand billing charges a fixed rate with no commitment and no interruption risk (outside of provider-side outages), and is the default rate quoted throughout this report unless otherwise noted. Spot or preemptible billing offers a substantial discount, typically 40% to 60%, in exchange for the provider's right to reclaim the instance with little or no notice when it needs the capacity back; AIMultiple's spot-discount tracker finds that "over the past six months, modern [GPU category] saves ~50%" versus on-demand pricing [1]. Reserved or committed-use billing locks in a lower rate in exchange for a fixed term, typically 1, 3, or 5 years, and is where the largest single discounts appear, GCP's 3-year commitment cuts its A3 Mega H100 rate by roughly 57%, as shown above, and Nebius's preemptible H100 tier prices at $2.15/hr against a $3.85/hr on-demand rate, a 44% discount [4].

...

results.title: Nebius выиграет от 20%-ного повышения цен Amazon на GPU
highlights:
Nebius Group позиционируется как один из главных бенефициаров повышения Amazon цен на аренду GPU-мощностей на 20%, которое вступило в силу 1 июля 2026 года. Аналитики видят в этом стимул для предприятий искать более дешёвые альтернативы — как раз то, что предлагает Nebius через оптимизированные решения и поддержку открытых моделей.

## Рост цен на AWS и реакция рынка

26 июня Amazon Web Services (AWS) уведомил клиентов об увеличении тарифов примерно на 20% для сервиса EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML — запланированных резервирований вычислительных мощностей на базе GPU NVIDIA. Изменения вступили в силу 1 июля. Это второе повышение цен за последние шесть месяцев: с декабря совокупный рост составил около 38%. Подорожание затронуло акселераторы P6-B300, стоимость аренды которых достигла 14,04 доллара в час, и мощности P5, цена на которые в регионах США составила 5,19 доллара в час. Другие варианты покупки остались без изменений, а собственный чип Amazon Trainium исключили из-под действия новых тарифов.

...

Аналитик также указал, что недавнее 20-процентное повышение цен Amazon на услуги резервирования GPU будет выгодно «неооблачным» провайдерам, таким как Nebius. Предприятия продолжают искать более дешёвые альтернативы, и Nebius предоставляет их через поддержку открытых моделей. По словам эксперта, это может стать катализатором нового роста акций NBIS.

results.title: Is the AI Chip Shortage Over in 2026? H100 Rentals Down 75%, HBM Backlogs Hit 52 Weeks | Value Add VC
highlights:
Quick Answer

H100 GPUs rent for $2.69 to $6.16 per GPU-hour on six providers' published price lists as of October 16, 2026, and B200s for $6.69 to $8.60 on demand. The AI chip shortage is not over: Nebius raised its H100 rate 53% between May and October.

An Nvidia H100 rents for $2.69 to $6.16 per GPU-hour as of October 16, 2026, across six providers' published price lists, and the cheapest B200 lists at $6.69. Those prices went up this year, not down, which is the clearest sign the AI chip shortage is not over.

...

No. GPU pricing in October 2026 says the AI chip shortage is still on: listed H100 rates run $2.69 to $6.16 per GPU-hour, on-demand B200 rates $6.69 to $8.60, and both list prices and market rents rose during 2026, even for H100s that first shipped in volume four years ago. Cheaper compute would show up as falling rents, and rents rose.

The best single data point is Nebius. Its pricing page showed the H100 at $2.95 an hour in early May; after an October 1 increase the same chip costs $4.50, and its B300 went from $6.10 to $9.50, according to The Motley Fool, which put the two increases at about 53% and 56% in five months. The same report says Nebius's second-quarter shareholder letter cited more than 30% higher pricing for older-generation GPUs versus the first quarter. The $4.50 H100 rate is live on Nebius's price list today.

## How much does an H100 cost per hour?

The median of the six providers' cheapest on-demand H100 SXM rates is $4.25 per GPU-hour (Value Add VC's arithmetic on the table below, taking one rate per provider). Specialist GPU clouds sit at the low end and the two node-priced sellers, CoreWeave and AWS, at the top.

## How much does a B200 cost per hour?

A B200 costs $6.69 to $8.60 per GPU-hour on demand, or $14.21 on reserved AWS Capacity Blocks, a median of $8.35 across six providers (Value Add VC's arithmetic). That is roughly twice the H100 median. Rack-scale GB200 NVL72 capacity, where 72 GPUs share one NVLink domain, prices near $10.50 per GPU.

| AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks | GB200 (u-p6e UltraServer) | $10.58 | $761.904 per 72-GPU UltraServer |

...

## Why are GPU rental prices rising in 2026?

Rents climbed across chip generations in 2026. Silicon Data figures cited by Wccftech on August 3, 2026 put the H100's market rental rate just shy of $2 an hour in January and approaching $3 by August, while B200 rates moved from just below $5 to $5.50 to $5.80. Those index figures sit below the list prices in the tables above because they track transacted and marketplace rates rather than rate cards.

The newest chips tightened fastest. Market strategist Warren Pies posted that B200 rental rates were up 30% year to date and called demand "insatiable," with availability at 0% in his own index, TIKR reported on September 29, 2026.

Memory is the other squeeze. High-bandwidth memory (HBM) is stacked on every data-center GPU, and its scarcity is now moving chip prices. KED Global reported on August 24, 2026 that Nvidia is raising prices for its AI accelerators amid a surge in memory chip prices. Chinese chipmakers including Huawei and Cambricon are also raising accelerator prices because HBM has become scarce, with Huawei's Ascend 950DT reportedly quoted 20% to 50% above earlier pricing, per Reuters reporting summarized by Yahoo Finance.

...

Interruptible capacity is far cheaper than on-demand. Together AI lists preemptible HGX H100 at $1.99 per GPU-hour against $3.99 on demand, and its reserved H100 rate falls from $3.69 for 3 to 30 days to $3.19 for 181 days or more, per its pricing page. CoreWeave lists an eight-GPU H100 spot node at $19.71 an hour, about $2.46 per GPU, and Nebius advertises spot H100 capacity from $0.79.

Commitments cut the B200 bill too: Together AI's B200 rate drops from $8.19 on demand to $6.79 on terms of 181 days or more, and Lambda's self-serve B200 at $6.69 already undercuts most providers' cluster pricing. For what those hourly rates mean per user or per token, see the true cost of running an AI product in 2026 and how inference costs per token have fallen even as GPU-hours got pricier.

...

For GPU clouds, rising rates lift the value of unsold capacity. Nebius had about $37.5 billion of remaining performance obligations at the end of June, more than 60 times its second-quarter revenue of $582 million, and those contracts were priced when signed, so the October increase does not reprice them, The Motley Fool noted in the same report.

results.title: GPU Rental Price 2026: What an H100-Hour Really Costs
highlights:
Strip a rented GPU-hour down to its cost basis and the hardware barely matters. At 70% fleet utilization, four-year amortization of a fully burdened H100 server comes to $1.12/hr, and energy plus facility adds another $0.33/hr — against a $3.99 on-demand price at Lambda. The residual $2.54/hr — 64% of the price — is demand premium: scarcity rent, not cost recovery (SA estimate). That premium splits the market into two pricing regimes. Neoclouds price per unit of compute: Lambda's B200 rents at 1.38x its H100 price for 2.27x the FP8 (sparse) throughput — about 39% cheaper per effective PFLOP. Hyperscalers price scarcity: AWS capacity blocks put B200 at 2.38x H100 — per-PFLOP parity, meaning the newest silicon carries zero performance discount. How fast reserved-tier discounts erode that premium is the most useful forward indicator of AI compute supply catching up with demand.

...

On Lambda's on-demand tier, a B200 runs $5.50/GPU-hour against $3.99 for an H100 — 1.38x the price for 2.27x the FP8 (sparse) throughput. Per unit of effective compute, the newest part is about 39% cheaper than the old one. On AWS capacity blocks — the same-tier comparison on the hyperscaler side — a B200 runs $9.36 against $3.93 for an H100: 2.38x the price for the same 2.27x the compute. Per-PFLOP parity. One market prices performance; the other prices a queue.

...

| SKU | Reference price (tier) | Hardware $/hr | Energy + facility $/hr | Demand premium $/hr | Premium share |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 SXM5 | $3.99 (Lambda, on-demand) | $1.12 | $0.33 | $2.54 | 63.7% |
| H200 | $3.89 (CoreWeave, on-demand) | $1.52 | $0.33 | $2.04 | 52.5% |
| B200 | $5.50 (Lambda, on-demand) | $1.60 | $0.47 | $3.43 | 62.4% |

...

On the neocloud side, Blackwell is a per-performance discount: Lambda's $5.50 B200 works out to $0.61 per effective FP8 (sparse) PFLOP-hour against $1.01 for its H100 — the 1.38x price buys 2.27x the compute. Hopper-class compute clusters around $1.00/PFLOP-hr regardless of provider tier: Lambda H100 on-demand $1.01, AWS H100 capacity block $0.99, CoreWeave H200 on-demand $0.98. That convergence is what a competitive market looks like.

On the hyperscaler side, AWS prices its B200 capacity blocks at $1.04 per FP8 (sparse) PFLOP-hour — 4.7% above its own H100 capacity block. Two years of silicon progress, zero per-performance discount. The H200 capacity block is worse still at $1.26 — a 27% per-PFLOP surcharge over H100 for the same compute plus more memory (141 GB vs. 80 GB), a premium AWS raised ~15% in January 2026 according to its published capacity-block prices. And hyperscaler on-demand tiers sit in a different universe entirely: Azure's on-demand H100 works out to $3.11 per FP8 (sparse) PFLOP-hour and GCP's to $2.77 — roughly 3x the neocloud level for identical silicon (all per-PFLOP figures SA estimates).

...

If the premium is scarcity rent, then the discounts providers offer for term commitments are their own forecast of how fast that scarcity decays:

| Provider | Spot discount | 1-yr reserved | 3-yr reserved |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AWS | 50-90% off | 25-31% off | Up to 45% off |
| Azure | ~20-30% off | ~30% off | ~40-50% off |
| GCP | 60-91% off | ~30% off | ~55% off |
| CoreWeave | N/A | Up to 60% off | Up to 60% off |

Source: provider public pricing documentation, Apr 2026 snapshot.

...

There is also direct evidence that premiums reprice administratively, not with costs: AWS cut on-demand H100 prices 44% in June 2025, then raised H200 capacity-block prices ~15% in January 2026. Nothing in the hardware or energy stack moved even a cent in either event — the premium did all the work. Weigh renting against owning with these same constants in our Cluster TCO calculator.

highlights: Last week, Amazon Web Services (AWS) raised prices on its EC2 Capacity Block reservations for its most powerful Nvidia GPU instances by 20%, citing supply and demand dynamics. results.title: NVIDIA GPU Rental Prices Soar 48% as AI Faces Worst Compute Shortage in Five Years | Bit.Fan
highlights:
NVIDIA's latest Blackwell GPU rental prices have surged 48% in two months to $4.08/hour, driven by an unprecedented AI compute crunch. Anthropic and OpenAI are hit hard, with OpenAI shutting down its video app Sora. Analysts expect the supply-demand imbalance to persist until at least 2029.

The artificial intelligence industry is facing its worst compute shortage in five years, with NVIDIA's latest Blackwell GPU rental prices surging 48% over the past two months to $4.08 per hour.

...

Several cloud providers have reported frequent offline incidents for GPU rental services, with some products being pulled entirely. Anthropic's Claude API, for instance, has seen its uptime fall below industry standards, impacting customer satisfaction. OpenAI is also grappling with massive demand—its API token processing volumes have more than doubled since last year, compelling the company to make difficult trade-offs, including the shutdown of its video generation app Sora.

results.title: Fly.io Kills GPU Hosting on August 1, 2026: Where the Workloads Go, and What It Actually Costs | bex.co
highlights:
On July 31, 2026, every GPU Machine on Fly.io stops being billable. On August 1, they stop existing. Fly's own docs now carry a single blunt line at the top of every GPU page: "GPUs are deprecated and will be unavailable after August 1." No grace period beyond that date, no grandfathered pricing, no quiet sunset — a hard stop for every team that built an inference endpoint, a fine-tuning job, or a document-processing pipeline on Fly GPU Machines.

...

Fly's GPU rates, as billed until the shutdown, were never expensive: $0.75/hour for an A10, $0.70/hour for an L40S, $1.25/hour for an A100 40G PCIe, $1.50/hour for an A100 80G SXM, billed by the second on top of the underlying Machine. Whatever you migrate to gets measured against that baseline.

There are exactly two kinds of destination, and they don't cost the same way:

Rental marketplaces — RunPod, Modal, Google Cloud Run GPU — sell GPU-hours the same way Fly did, just without the exit risk (for now).

| Provider | GPU | Rate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| RunPod Secure Cloud | RTX 6000 Ada (48GB) | $0.77/hr |
| RunPod Secure Cloud | A100 80G SXM | $1.49/hr |
| Modal | A100 80G | ~$2.50/hr |
| Google Cloud Run | L4 (24GB) | ~$0.67/hr |

Owned hardware — a dedicated GPU box you rack under your own control plane instead of renting someone else's — is priced flat, by the month, regardless of how many hours you actually use it. Hetzner's two dedicated GPU servers, the closest thing to an "own it instead" option for a Cluster-API-managed fleet:

...

For the RTX-class tier Hetzner does sell, run the actual break-even math before assuming ownership wins. A GEX130 costs about $935/month, which is $1.28/hour amortized over a full 730-hour month. RunPod's Secure Cloud rents the same RTX 6000 Ada for $0.77/hour. Run it every hour of every day for a month and the rental bill is $562 — still $373 cheaper than owning the box outright. At 100% utilization, for one team's workload, renting still beats owning. That's the opposite of the usual "buy hardware once utilization gets high enough" intuition, and it's worth stating plainly instead of assuming the math works out the way owned-infrastructure pitches usually claim it does.

results.title: Enterprise GPU FOMO Tax: Mid-Market AI Cost Discipline in 2026
highlights:
That number does not describe a few outlier deployments. It describes the default state of enterprise GPU infrastructure in 2026. And it lands at the same moment that AWS quietly raised reserved H200 prices by roughly fifteen percent in January, HBM3e memory pushed up another twenty percent for the year, and TSMC's advanced packaging — the bottleneck that gates every modern GPU — booked through mid-2027. According to the same VB analysis, this is the first time since AWS launched EC2 in 2006 that a hyperscaler has meaningfully raised reserved GPU pricing rather than cut it. The standing assumption inside most enterprise AI budgets — that compute gets cheaper every year — has stopped being true at the top of the stack.

...

- Cast AI measured enterprise GPU fleets at roughly 5% utilization in production, against a reasonable human-managed target of around 30%.
- AWS raised reserved H200 prices roughly 15% in January with no formal announcement — the first meaningful hyperscaler GPU price hike since EC2 launched in 2006.
- Cloud compute has split in two: commodity tier prices keep falling, frontier tier prices are rising as Nvidia takes orders for 2 million H200s against 700,000 in inventory.
- Four FOMO procurement patterns are visible in mid-market AI buying — locked allocations, oversized model deployments, redundant vendor contracts, and “AI sandbox” environments nobody touches.
- A six-question self-audit exposes most of the FOMO spend before the next renewal cycle.
- Some excess capacity is necessary for burst usage; the discipline is knowing your actual P95 utilization, not eliminating headroom.
